claim: Infertility affects 10% to 15% (approximately 186 million) of couples at reproductive age around the world.
source: Infertility is increasingly becoming a global health issue that affects 10% to 15% (e.g., approximately 186 million) of couples at reproductive age around the world (Inhorn and Patrizio, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Inhorn and Patrizio, 2015.

claim: Some female patients with primary infertility suffer from oocyte maturation arrest, premature oocyte death, fertilization failure, or preimplantation embryonic arrest.
source: These female patients with primary infertility were most often attributed to functional deficiency in the oocytes, such as oocyte maturation arrest, premature oocyte death, fertilization failure, or preimplantation embryonic arrest (Sang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sang et al., 2021.

claim: Oocyte maturation is referred to as meiotic resumption of oocytes from the germinal vesicle (GV) to the metaphase II (MII) stage.
source: Oocyte maturation is referred to as meiotic resumption of oocytes from the germinal vesicle (GV) to the metaphase II (MII) stage in vivo or in vitro, whereby the oocytes acquire the developmental competence.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Oocyte maturation arrest is characterized by the frequent occurrence of oocytes mostly or entirely arrested at the GV or metaphase I (MI) stage.
source: In the clinic, oocyte maturation arrest is characterized by the frequent occurrence of oocytes mostly or entirely arrested at the GV or metaphase I (MI) stage, representing a rare but highly challenging disease for treatment through traditional ART (Mehlmann, 2005; Mrazek and Fulka, 2003; Beall et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mehlmann, 2005; Mrazek and Fulka, 2003; Beall et al., 2010.

claim: Female germ cells initiate meiosis during embryonic development once primordial germ cells transit and colonize the genital ridge in mice and humans.
source: Unlike the male germline, female germ cells initiate meiosis very early during embryonic development once primordial germ cells transit and colonize the genital ridge in mice and humans (Hilscher et al., 1974; McLaren, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hilscher et al., 1974; McLaren, 2003.

claim: Oocytes remain arrested at the diplotene stage in meiotic prophase I during postnatal oocyte growth in growing follicles.
source: Nonetheless, following the synapsis and recombination between homologous chromosomes, meiotic progression ceases in the embryonic gonad, and the oocytes remain arrested at the diplotene stage in meiotic prophase I during postnatal oocyte growth in growing follicles (McLaren, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McLaren, 2003.

claim: Fully grown oocytes acquire the ability to resume meiotic division upon luteinizing hormone surge.
source: This process is concurrent with the oocyte cytoplasmic and meiotic maturation process whereby the oocytes continuously grow with increased size and acquire the ability to resume meiotic division upon luteinizing hormone surge (Mehlmann, 2005; Park et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mehlmann, 2005; Park et al., 2004.

claim: Meiotic resumption is characterized by chromatin condensation and the dissolution of nuclear membranes, termed 'GV breakdown' (GVBD).
source: Morphologically, meiotic resumption is characterized by chromatin condensation and the dissolution of nuclear membranes, termed 'GV breakdown' (GVBD).
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Genetic ablation of Marf1, Cdc25b, or Pde3a led to GV arrest in mouse oocytes.
source: For instance, genetic ablation of Marf1, Cdc25b, or Pde3a led to GV arrest (Su et al., 2012; Lincoln et al., 2002; Masciarelli et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Su et al., 2012; Lincoln et al., 2002; Masciarelli et al., 2004.

claim: Deletion of Ccnb3, Cks2, or Mlh1 caused MI arrest in mouse oocytes.
source: while deletion of Ccnb3, Cks2, or Mlh1 caused MI arrest in mouse oocytes (Karasu et al., 2019; Spruck et al., 2003; Woods et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karasu et al., 2019; Spruck et al., 2003; Woods et al., 1999.

claim: Mouse oocytes deficient in Mlh3 arrested at both the MI and MII stages.
source: For example, mouse oocytes deficient in Mlh3 arrested at both the MI and MII stages (Lipkin et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lipkin et al., 2002.

claim: Ubb-null oocytes ceased at both the GV and MI stages.
source: whereas Ubb-null oocytes ceased at both the GV and MI stages (Ryu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ryu et al., 2008.

claim: Only a limited number of protein-coding variants have been discovered to account for human oocyte maturation arrest, including TUBB8, PATL2, and TRIP13.
source: Until recently, only a limited number of protein-coding variants have been discovered to account for human oocyte maturation arrest, including TUBB8 (Feng et al., 2016) (MIM: 616768), PATL2 (Maddirevula et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018) (MIM:614661), and TRIP13 (Zhang et al., 2020) (MIM: 604507).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feng et al., 2016; Maddirevula et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Mutations in TUBB8, PATL2, and TRIP13 can only account for a very small proportion (<30%) of patients with oocyte maturation arrest syndrome.
source: However, mutations in these genes can only account for a very small proportion (<30%) of patients with this syndrome, and the deleterious causative variants in most cases remain largely unknown (Feng et al., 2016; Maddirevula et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020; Christou-Kent et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feng et al., 2016; Maddirevula et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020; Christou-Kent et al., 2018.

claim: MAD2L1BP (p31comet) physically interacts with MAD2 through a conformation-specific binding.
source: MAD2L1-binding protein (MAD2L1BP) (MIM: 618136), also called p31comet, mimicking the structure of mitosis arrest deficient 2 (MAD2), physically interacts with MAD2 through a conformation-specific binding and it functions as an adapter between MAD2 and TRIP13 (Yang et al., 2007; Alfieri et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2007; Alfieri et al., 2018.

claim: MAD2L1BP functions as an adapter between MAD2 and TRIP13.
source: MAD2L1-binding protein (MAD2L1BP) (MIM: 618136), also called p31comet, mimicking the structure of mitosis arrest deficient 2 (MAD2), physically interacts with MAD2 through a conformation-specific binding and it functions as an adapter between MAD2 and TRIP13 (Yang et al., 2007; Alfieri et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2007; Alfieri et al., 2018.

claim: Timely disassembly of the MCC and silencing of the SAC rely on the joint action of both p31comet and TRIP13 in mitosis.
source: In mitosis, timely disassembly of the MCC and hence the silencing of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) rely on the joint action of both p31comet and TRIP13 (Alfieri et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alfieri et al., 2018.

claim: Whole-body p31comet knockout mice die soon after birth and have reduced hepatic glycogen.
source: Whole-body p31comet knockout mice die soon after birth and have reduced hepatic glycogen (Choi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Choi et al., 2016.

claim: P31comet plays an important role in meiosis in rice.
source: In rice, P31comet plays an important role in meiosis.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript text.

claim: The P31comet mutant rice was normal in vegetative growth but showed complete sterility.
source: The P31comet mutant rice was normal in vegetative growth but showed complete sterility (Ji et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ji et al., 2016.

claim: Homozygous and compound heterozygous MAD2L1BP variants were identified in three families with female patients diagnosed with primary infertility owing to oocyte MI arrest.
source: In this study, by whole-exome sequencing (WES), we identified homozygous and compound heterozygous MAD2L1BP variants in three families with female patients diagnosed with primary infertility owing to oocyte metaphase I (MI) arrest.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on WES data.

claim: The protein variants resulting from the C-terminal truncation of MAD2L1BP lost their binding ability to MAD2.
source: Functional studies revealed that the protein variants resulting from the C-terminal truncation of MAD2L1BP lost their binding ability to MAD2.
evidence: This is a finding from functional studies (Co-IP assays) presented in the manuscript.

claim: cRNA microinjection of full-length or truncated MAD2L1BP uncovered their discordant roles in driving the extrusion of polar body 1 (PB1) in mouse oocytes.
source: cRNA microinjection of full-length or truncated MAD2L1BP uncovered their discordant roles in driving the extrusion of polar body 1 (PB1) in mouse oocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from microinjection experiments in mouse oocytes presented in the manuscript.

claim: The patient's oocytes carrying the mutated MAD2L1BP resumed polar body extrusion (PBE) when rescued by microinjection of full-length MAD2L1BP cRNAs.
source: Furthermore, the patient's oocytes carrying the mutated MAD2L1BP resumed polar body extrusion (PBE) when rescued by microinjection of full-length MAD2L1BP cRNAs.
evidence: This is a finding from rescue experiments in human patient oocytes presented in the manuscript.

claim: Biallelic variants in MAD2L1BP are responsible for human oocyte maturation arrest at MI.
source: Together, our studies identified and characterized novel biallelic variants in MAD2L1BP responsible for human oocyte maturation arrest at MI, and thus prompted new therapeutic avenues for curing female primary infertility.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on genetic, functional, and rescue data.

claim: A cohort of 50 female patients with primary infertility displaying oocyte maturation arrest at the MI stage was recruited.
source: A cohort of 50 female patients with primary infertility displaying the oocyte maturation arrest at the MI stage was recruited from the Reproductive Center of the First Affiliated Hospital of USTC (University of Science and Technology of China) and the Reproductive Hospital at Shandong University between July 2014 and October 2021.
evidence: This describes the patient cohort used in the study.

claim: All the patients had normal karyotypes (46, XX).
source: All the patients had normal karyotypes (46, XX) and had undergone at least one cycle of IVF or ICSI treatment
evidence: This is a characteristic of the patient cohort.

claim: Two homozygous nonsense variants (c.853C>T [p.R285*] and c.541C>T [p.R181*]) of MAD2L1BP were identified from two unrelated families (Family 1 and Family 3).
source: This pipeline analyses led us to narrow down the candidate variants to a short list in three families (12, 14, and 11 candidate genes in the respective families) (Table 2, Table 2—source data 1), and eventually to focus on one shared gene variant, namely MAD2L1BP, wherein two homozygous nonsense variants (c.853C>T [p.R285*] and c.541C>T [p.R181*]) of MAD2L1BP from two unrelated families (Family 1 and Family 3), respectively
evidence: This is a finding from WES analysis.

claim: Two compound heterozygous variants (a frameshift mutation p.F173Sfs4* and an intronic mutation c.21-94G>A) of MAD2L1BP were identified in Family 2.
source: and two compound heterozygous variants (a frameshift mutation p.F173Sfs4* and an intronic mutation c.21-94G>A) of MAD2L1BP in Family 2 (Table 2—source data 1, Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from WES analysis.

claim: In Family 1, the female patient (F1: II-1) underwent three unsuccessful cycles of IVF with 29 out of 30 superovulated oocytes arrested at the MI stage.
source: In the first case, the female patient (F1: II-1) was from a consanguineous family and underwent three unsuccessful cycles of IVF with 29 out of a total of 30 superovulated oocytes arrested at the MI stage (Figure 1A, Figure 1C, Table 1).
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient.

claim: WES analysis identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in NM_001003690 (MAD2L1BP): c.853C>T [p.R285*] in Family 1.
source: WES analysis following a set of bioinformatic pipelines identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in NM_001003690 (MAD2L1BP): c.853C>T [p.R285*] (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from WES analysis.

claim: The younger brother (F1: II-2) of the female patient in Family 1 carried the same homozygous mutation.
source: Her younger brother (F1: II-2), 22 years of age, carried the same homozygous mutation (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from genetic analysis.

claim: The consanguineous parents in Family 1 were both heterozygous for the c.853C>T mutation.
source: Further Sanger sequencing after PCR amplification confirmed that their consanguineous parents were both heterozygous for this mutation.
evidence: This is a finding from Sanger sequencing.

claim: In Family 2, the patient (F2: II-1) had one cycle of IVF with all nine collected oocytes arrested at MI.
source: The second patient was diagnosed with primary infertility with no history of consanguinity. She had gone through one cycle of IVF, and all nine collected oocytes were arrested at MI (F2: II-1) (Figure 1C, Table 1).
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient.

claim: A heterozygous frameshift mutation c.518delT [p.F173Sfs4*] in MAD2L1BP was uncovered by WES in Family 2.
source: A heterozygous frameshift mutation c.518delT [p.F173Sfs4*] in MAD2L1BP was uncovered by WES (Figure 1A,Table 3), which was inherited from her mother.
evidence: This is a finding from WES analysis.

claim: A heterozygous intronic variant c.21–94G>A in MAD2L1BP was validated in the patient (F2: II-1) by Sanger sequencing.
source: Subsequent Sanger sequencing of ~200 bp intron-flanking sequences of MAD2L1BP validated a heterozygous intronic variant c.21–94G>A in the patient (F2: II-1), which was transmitted from her father (Figure 1A–C, Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from Sanger sequencing.

claim: In Family 3, the female patient had five superovulated oocytes all arrested at MI after two unsuccessful cycles of IVF.
source: In the third family, the female patient had a total of five superovulated oocytes all arrested at MI after two unsuccessful cycles of IVF.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient.

claim: WES and subsequent PCR sequencing revealed a homozygous mutation c.541C>T [p.R181*] in MAD2L1BP in Family 3.
source: WES and subsequent PCR sequencing revealed a homozygous mutation c.541C>T [p.R181*] in MAD2L1BP (Figure 1A and B, Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from WES and PCR sequencing.

claim: The c.541C>T mutation in Family 3 was inherited from her parents respectively.
source: This mutation was inherited from her parents respectively and likely resulted in the production of a much shorter C-terminally truncated MAD2L1BP protein compared with p.R285* variant from the first patient (F1: II-1).
evidence: This is a finding from genetic analysis.

claim: The nonsense variants p.R285* and p.R181* occurred at low allele frequencies (3/248598 and 2/250850, respectively) in the gnomAD browser.
source: The nonsense variants p.R285* and p.R181* occurred at low allele frequencies (3/248598 and 2/250850, respectively) in the gnomAD browser
evidence: This is data from the gnomAD database.

claim: The frameshift mutation p.F173Sfs4* was not found in the gnomAD database.
source: and the frameshift mutation p.F173Sfs4* was not found in the database (Table 3).
evidence: This is data from the gnomAD database.

claim: The intronic variant c.21-94G>A (rs142226267) had an allele frequency of 111/31250 and homozygote frequency of 2/31250 in the gnomAD browser.
source: However, the intronic variant c.21-94G>A (rs142226267) had an allele frequency of 111/31250 and homozygote frequency of 2/31250 in the gnomAD browser, which was initially filtered out through the WES analysis pipeline but subsequently reconsidered for further evaluation of its pathogenicity (Table 3).
evidence: This is data from the gnomAD database.

claim: The nonsense variants p.R285* and p.R181* and the frameshift mutation p.F173Sfs4* gave rise to a premature termination codon (PTC) in the resultant MAD2L1BP mRNA.
source: The nonsense variants p.R285* and p.R181* and the frameshift mutation p.F173Sfs4* gave rise to a premature termination codon (PTC) in the resultant MAD2L1BP mRNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of nonsense and frameshift mutations.

claim: The intronic variant c.21-94G>A was predicted to be a cryptic splicing acceptor site of exon 2 by NNsplice and ASSP.
source: For the intronic variant c.21-94G>A, it was predicted to be a cryptic splicing acceptor site of exon 2 by NNsplice and ASSP, presumably leading to aberrant splicing of Exon 2 with additional intronic sequences resulting in a PTC introduction (Table 3).
evidence: This is a prediction from bioinformatic tools (NNsplice and ASSP).

claim: MAD2L1BP is a relatively small-sized protein consisting of only 306 amino acids.
source: MAD2L1BP is a relatively small-sized protein consisting of only 306 amino acids, which are highly evolutionarily conserved across metazoan species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on protein sequence analysis.

claim: MAD2L1BP is highly evolutionarily conserved across metazoan species.
source: MAD2L1BP is a relatively small-sized protein consisting of only 306 amino acids, which are highly evolutionarily conserved across metazoan species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on evolutionary conservation analysis shown in figures.

claim: There is a shorter isoform of MAD2L1BP that differs exclusively at the N-terminus compared to the longer isoform in humans.
source: Interestingly, there is a shorter isoform that differs exclusively at the N-terminus compared to the longer isoform in humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MAD2L1BP mRNAs are highly abundant in both human and mouse oocytes, especially those at advanced stages.
source: By analyzing the published RNA-seq databases, we found that MAD2L1BP mRNAs are highly abundant in both human and mouse oocytes, especially those at advanced stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on analysis of published RNA-seq databases.

claim: The p.R285* mutation did not affect the expression levels of MAD2L1BP mRNAs in the first patient (F1: II-1).
source: We discovered that p.R285* mutation did not affect the expression levels of MAD2L1BP mRNAs in the first patient (F1: II-1) (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The p.R285* mutation possibly produces a truncated MAD2L1BP protein with loss of C-terminal 22 amino acids.
source: thus possibly producing a truncated MAD2L1BP protein loss of C-terminal 22 amino acids (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of the nonsense mutation.

claim: The aberrant splicing around Exon 2 was repeatedly observed by sequencing the transcribed spliced mRNA product after transfection of the c.21-94G>A variant construct into 293T cells in vitro.
source: Not surprisingly, the aberrant splicing around Exon 2 was repeatedly observed by sequencing the transcribed spliced mRNA product after transfection into 293T cells in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on in vitro splicing assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MAD2L1BP mRNA levels were significantly reduced in the blood from the second patient (F2: II-1).
source: In support of this finding, the qPCR assay validated that the MAD2L1BP mRNA levels were significantly reduced in the blood from the second patient (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The p.R181* mutation would only be possible to generate a much shorter MAD2L1BP protein than p.R285* variant, leading to a complete loss of 126 amino acids at the C-terminus.
source: However, the p.R181* mutation would only be possible to generate a much shorter MAD2L1BP protein than p.R285* variant in the first patient (F1: II-1), leading to a complete loss of 126 amino acids at the C-terminus (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of the nonsense mutation.

claim: The truncated MAD2L1BP MUT (p.R285*) lost interaction with MAD2 when co-transfected into 293T cells in vitro.
source: Not surprisingly, while the Flag-tagged WT MAD2L1BP could strongly pull down the full-length MAD2 as judged by Co-IP, the loss of 22 aa in MAD2L1BP at the C-terminus completely abolished its binding to MAD2, suggesting an essential function of the C-terminal 22 aa in stabilizing the binding of MAD2L1BP to MAD2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on Co-IP assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The C-terminal 22 residues of MAD2L1BP fold into the β9 and β10 strands, which are in charge of the physical interaction between MAD2L1BP and MAD2.
source: In support of this finding, the resolved crystal structure of MAD2L1BP (PDB: 2QYF) showed that its C-terminal 22 residues fold into the β9 and β10 strands, which are in charge of the physical interaction between MAD2L1BP and MAD2 like a seatbelt essential for the conformational stability (Yang et al., 2007; Figures 1B and 2F).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure data (PDB: 2QYF) and citation to Yang et al., 2007.

claim: Exogenous expression of either WT or p.R285* Mad2l1bp resulted in similar percentages of oocytes undergoing GVBD.
source: As shown in Figure 3B and C, exogenous expression of either WT or p.R285* Mad2l1bp alone resulted in similar percentages of oocytes undergoing GVBD.
evidence: This is based on microinjection experiments in mouse oocytes shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Microinjection of the WT Mad2l1bp cRNAs accelerated the polar body extrusion (PBE) by ~3 hr as compared with control groups.
source: A quantitative comparison from the time-lapse imaging experiments revealed that microinjection of the WT Mad2l1bp cRNAs accelerated the polar body extrusion (PBE) by ~3 hr as compared with those in the control groups (non-injected or GFP cRNA group), although the resultant percentages of oocytes with PBE were comparable among WT Mad2l1bp and control groups (~80%) (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging experiments shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: Supplementation with p.R285* Mad2l1bp cRNAs not only postponed the extrusion of the polar body but also significantly lowered the final PBE rate in the oocytes (~40%).
source: By comparison, supplementation with p.R285* Mad2l1bp cRNAs not only postponed the extrusion of the polar body but also significantly lowered the final PBE rate in the oocytes (~40%) (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging experiments shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: The majority of GV oocytes supplemented with the WT Mad2l1bp cRNAs developed beyond meiosis I, as judged by the PBE.
source: Consistently, the majority of GV oocytes supplemented with the WT Mad2l1bp cRNAs developed beyond meiosis I, as judged by the PBE (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments in mouse oocytes shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The oocytes supplemented with the p.R285* Mad2l1bp cRNAs rarely extruded the polar body.
source: In contrast, the oocytes supplemented with the p.R285* Mad2l1bp cRNAs rarely extruded the polar body, suggesting that the oocyte maturation was impeded at the MI stage, and the MAD2L1BP variant lost its function in vivo as compared with its WT counterpart (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments in mouse oocytes shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: In the oocytes co-injected with p.R285* Mad2l1bp cRNA, persistent Bub3-positive staining was observed in the kinetochore of bivalent chromosome spreads throughout in vitro maturation.
source: In the oocytes co-injected with p.R285* Mad2l1bp cRNA, we observed persistent Bub3-positive staining in the kinetochore of bivalent chromosome spreads throughout in vitro maturation, indicating activated SAC response in the presence of p.R285* Mad2l1bp variant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The oocytes co-injected with Mad2l1bp WT predominantly harbored univalent chromosomes (~85%) and much lower intensity of Bub3-positive staining.
source: In contrast, the oocytes co-injected with Mad2l1bp WT predominantly harbored univalent chromosomes (~85%) and much lower intensity of Bub3-positive staining, indicative of the SAC silence and completion of meiotic division I (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four out of six oocytes from the first patient (F1: II-1) extruded PB1 after microinjection with full-length MAD2L1BP cRNAs.
source: Intriguingly, we attained four oocytes with PB1 after culture in G-MOPS medium for in vitro maturation, indicative of the successful completion of meiosis I in the patient's oocytes when supplemented with exogenous intact MAD2L1BP cRNAs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments in human patient oocytes shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The other two recovered oocytes with sham microinjection failed to extrude the polar body as a control.
source: In contrast, the other two recovered oocytes with sham microinjection failed to extrude the polar body as a control (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on control experiments in human patient oocytes shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The brother of the female patient from Family 1 was also infertile.
source: Of note, the brother of the female patient from Family 1 (Figure 1A) was also infertile.
evidence: This is clinical information about the patient's brother.

claim: Examination of the brother's semen sample showed that he had a markedly declined number of sperm, some of which exhibit aberrant head morphology.
source: Examination of his semen sample showed that he had a markedly declined number of sperm, some of which exhibit aberrant head morphology, reminiscent of a possible role of MAD2L1BP in spermatogenesis as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on semen analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: 1811 transcripts were down-regulated while 1705 transcripts were up-regulated in MAD2L1BPR285* oocytes.
source: Among them, we discovered that 1811 transcripts were down-regulated while 1705 transcripts were up-regulated in MAD2L1BPR285* oocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The down-regulated transcripts in MAD2L1BPR285* oocytes were mainly engaged in pathways related to cell division and cell cycle.
source: The Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed that, in support of the phenotypic meiotic arrest, the down-regulated transcripts were mainly engaged in pathways related to cell division and cell cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The transcript expression levels for MCC components, including MAD2, BUBR1, and CDC20 (except BUB3), as well as TRIP13 were comparable between MAD2L1BPR285* and control oocytes.
source: Interestingly, the transcript expression levels for MCC components, including MAD2, BUBR1, and CDC20 (except BUB3), as well as TRIP13 were comparable between MAD2L1BPR285* and control oocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), which is consistent with previous studies and our qPCR experiments (Figure 2C; Ma and Poon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and citation to Ma and Poon, 2016.

claim: The expression levels of other cell division-related factors were significantly decreased in MAD2L1BPR285* oocytes.
source: However, the expression levels of other cell division-related factors were significantly decreased in MAD2L1BPR285* oocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The up-regulated transcripts in MAD2L1BPR285* oocytes were predominantly relevant to mitochondrial metabolism.
source: Intriguingly, the GO analysis unveiled that the up-regulated transcripts were predominantly relevant to mitochondrial metabolism, which is critical for energy homeostasis during oocyte maturation (Richani et al., 2021; Trebichalská et al., 2021; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and G).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and G, and citations to Richani et al., 2021; Trebichalská et al., 2021.

claim: The SAC is an intricate surveillance mechanism that ensures accurate segregation of chromosomes throughout cell cycles.
source: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) is an intricate surveillance mechanism that ensures accurate segregation of chromosomes throughout cell cycles.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the SAC.

claim: Once the kinetochores of chromosomes are correctly attached to bipolar spindles and the SAC is satisfied, the MAD2L1BP binds MAD2 and recruits the AAA+-ATPase TRIP13 to disassemble the MCC.
source: Once the kinetochores of chromosomes are correctly attached to bipolar spindles and the SAC is satisfied, the MAD2L1BP, best known as p31comet, binds mitosis arrest deficient 2 (MAD2) and recruits the AAA+-ATPase TRIP13 to disassemble the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC), leading to the cell-cycle progression.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MAD2L1BP function.

claim: The SAC represses the downstream anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) activity until all chromosomes are correctly aligned and attached to the bipolar spindles through the kinetochores.
source: To ensure the fidelity of chromosome segregation, the cells, including the oocytes, have evolved an exquisite surveillance machinery – the SAC, which represses the downstream anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) activity until all chromosomes are correctly aligned and attached to the bipolar spindles through the kinetochores (Mihajlović and FitzHarris, 2018; Liu and Zhang, 2016; Charalambous et al., 2023; Vallot et al., 2018; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mihajlović and FitzHarris, 2018; Liu and Zhang, 2016; Charalambous et al., 2023; Vallot et al., 2018.

claim: The MCC is comprised of four core components: BUBR1, MAD2, BUB3, and the APC activator CDC20.
source: Central to the SAC is the physical presence of the MCC, which is comprised of four core components: BUBR1, MAD2, BUB3, and the APC activator CDC20.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the MCC composition.

claim: The MCC components are phylogenetically conserved in metazoan species.
source: These players are phylogenetically conserved in metazoan species, and mouse models have provided unambiguous evidence showing their indispensable roles in cell-cycle progression (Liu and Zhang, 2016; Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu and Zhang, 2016; Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021.

claim: The SAC activation drives the conversion of Mad2 from its inactive, open conformer (O-Mad2) to its closed, active form (C-Mad2) through a 'Mad1-Mad2 templating' mechanism.
source: This drives the conversion of Mad2 from its inactive, open conformer (O-Mad2) to its closed, active form (C-Mad2) through a generally accepted 'Mad1-Mad2 templating' mechanism for cytosolic propagation of spindle checkpoint signal (Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021.

claim: Inactivation of Mad2 caused the accelerated mitotic exit in somatic cells.
source: Genetic mouse models have shown that Mad2 is the core player of SAC signaling – inactivation of Mad2 caused the accelerated mitotic exit whereas overexpression of Mad2 induced precocious activation of SAC in somatic cells and meiotic MI arrest in oocytes, suggesting MAD2 is functional and required for normal oocyte meiotic progression (Wassmann et al., 2003; Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021; Niault et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wassmann et al., 2003; Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021; Niault et al., 2007.

claim: Overexpression of Mad2 induced precocious activation of SAC in somatic cells and meiotic MI arrest in oocytes.
source: Genetic mouse models have shown that Mad2 is the core player of SAC signaling – inactivation of Mad2 caused the accelerated mitotic exit whereas overexpression of Mad2 induced precocious activation of SAC in somatic cells and meiotic MI arrest in oocytes, suggesting MAD2 is functional and required for normal oocyte meiotic progression (Wassmann et al., 2003; Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021; Niault et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wassmann et al., 2003; Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2021; Niault et al., 2007.

claim: Once the kinetochore-spindle attachment is satisfactorily achieved, the inhibitory signaling from the SAC must be timely quenched to allow anaphase progression.
source: Once the kinetochore-spindle attachment is satisfactorily achieved, the inhibitory signaling from the SAC must be timely quenched to allow anaphase progression.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SAC function.

claim: SAC silencing is primarily achieved through MAD2 recognition by MAD2L1BP, which further recruits AAA+ATPase, TRIP13, that binds and subsequently dissembles the MCC in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: This is primarily achieved through MAD2 recognition by MAD2L1BP, which further recruits AAA+ATPase, TRIP13, that binds and subsequently dissembles the MCC in an ATP-dependent manner (Alfieri et al., 2018; Brulotte et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alfieri et al., 2018; Brulotte et al., 2017.

claim: Deficient SAC disassembly, such as MAD2L1BP mutations, disrupts the MAD2•MAD2L1BP(p31comet)•TRIP13 axis, leading to sustained SAC activation and oocyte maturation arrest.
source: Conversely, deficient SAC disassembly, for example, MAD2L1BP mutations in this study, disrupts the MAD2•MAD2L1BP(p31comet)•TRIP13 axis, leading to sustained SAC activation and consequently the oocyte maturation arrest (Figure 4B, lower panel).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of this study and established knowledge.

claim: Recent studies have identified pathogenic biallelic variants in TRIP13 causing female primary infertility owing to oocyte maturation arrest predominantly at MI stage.
source: Intriguingly, recent studies have identified pathogenic biallelic variants in TRIP13 causing female primary infertility owing to the oocyte maturation arrest predominantly at MI stage (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: A spectrum of deleterious variants in CDC20 have been discovered that account for human oocyte meiotic arrest and early embryonic failure.
source: Furthermore, a spectrum of deleterious variants in CDC20, the core component of MCC, have also been discovered, that account for human oocyte meiotic arrest and early embryonic failure (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: This study is the first report that identified and characterized causative loss-of-function variants in MAD2L1BP underlying human oocyte maturation arrest.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first report that identified and characterized causative loss-of-function variants in MAD2L1BP underlying human oocyte maturation arrest.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: MAD2L1BP KO cells exhibited mitotic delay and lagging chromosomes.
source: Consistent with the abnormalities in MAD2L1BP-null oocyte meiotic division, MAD2L1BP KO cells exhibited mitotic delay and lagging chromosomes (Ma and Poon, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ma and Poon, 2016.

claim: Some MAD2L1BP KO cells managed to reinitiate cell cycle, which is distinct from the complete arrest in the mutant oocytes.
source: but some of them managed to reinitiate cell cycle, which is distinct from the complete arrest in the mutant oocytes.
evidence: This is a comparison between somatic cells and oocytes based on the findings.

claim: Mad2l1bp-deficient mice died perinatally owing to neonatal hypoglycemia resulting from liver glycogen shortage.
source: However, Mad2l1bp-deficient mice died perinatally owing to the neonatal hypoglycemia resulting from the liver glycogen shortage, rendering us fail to get the homozygous KI offspring (Choi et al., 2016).

claim: This study adds novel pathogenic variants of MAD2L1BP to the genetic mutational spectrum underlying human oocyte maturation arrest.
source: Taken together, with a small-scale cohort of genetic screening in 50 oocyte MI-arrested patients, our study adds novel pathogenic variants of MAD2L1BP to the genetic mutational spectrum underlying human oocyte maturation arrest, and likely provides novel diagnostic and therapeutic avenues for primary female infertility in the future.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study.
